feature_request: Project managers should be able to see the full history of engagement with a country before starting a new mission.

proposed_scope_in: Read-only 'Country Engagement History' panel on the Country record and surfaced as a pre-flight step in the 'New Mission' creation flow, built from existing Engagement, Mission, Project, and Contact records

Single reverse-chronological timeline per country combining existing Engagement entries, past/active Missions, and Project affiliations, with each row showing date, type, summary, linked Contact name, and linked Mission/Project
Basic filters computed from existing fields only: date range, engagement type, and linked Project/Mission
Inline 'Active missions in this country' banner at the top of the panel, derived from existing Mission status
Permission inheritance: a user sees a timeline row only if they already have access to the underlying Engagement/Mission/Contact record under the existing access model
Contacts are displayed from existing links with their current Contact record data; no new contact-role tracking
Pagination (default 50 rows) and server-side query on existing indexed fields (country_id, date)
Non-blocking: the New Mission flow shows the history link/summary count but does not require PM acknowledgement or sign-off
Read-only CSV export is NOT included; view-only in UI
proposed_scope_out: Any new tables or entities (no new 'EngagementSummary', 'Relationship', or historical role-graph tables)
Backfill, cleanup, or normalization of legacy engagement data (history is shown as-is, with gaps visible)
New data-entry fields or required manual steps for Regional Coordinators
AI/ML summarization, sentiment scoring, 'relationship health' scores, or recommendations
Mandatory acknowledgement/approval gate before creating a mission
Custom RBAC, new classification/sensitivity tagging, or redaction workflows beyond existing access inheritance
Historical point-in-time contact roles (who held which role when)
Cross-country or regional rollups and multi-country comparisons
Export, print, or sharing of the history outside the CRM
Edit/annotate capabilities from the history view
Integration with external systems (email, calendar, ministry systems)
Notifications or alerts about history content

assumptions.statement: 'Full history' means all engagement records already stored in the CRM (Engagements, Missions, Project affiliations) for that country, not data from external systems or undocumented interactions.
assumptions.rationale: Limiting to existing records means zero ingestion work and no new data entry, so the team can ship in one cycle and Regional Coordinators are not asked for anything new.

assumptions.statement: Project managers are authenticated CRM users who already have some access to Country and Mission records; visibility of individual history rows follows existing record-level permissions rather than a new rule set.
assumptions.rationale: Inheriting the current access model avoids building RBAC and avoids deciding who may see what, which is an institutional policy call rather than a product one.

assumptions.statement: Engagement history is a read/orientation aid at the pre-mission planning stage, not a compliance control, so it is advisory and non-blocking.
assumptions.rationale: A non-blocking view avoids approval chains and workflow states, keeping the feature a query + UI change only.

assumptions.statement: Existing Engagement records carry a country link (directly or via Contact/Mission/Project) and a date, which is sufficient to assemble a timeline with a single query.
assumptions.rationale: Reusing existing relationships means no schema migration; where links are missing, the gap is displayed rather than fixed, so the MVP does not depend on data cleanup.

assumptions.statement: A country's history volume is manageable (hundreds to low thousands of rows) so pagination and standard indexes suffice without a precomputed summary store.
assumptions.rationale: Avoids caching/materialized views and extra infrastructure for v1; we can measure load time and add optimization later if needed.

assumptions.statement: Contacts shown in history reflect the contact's current record; people who changed roles or left are displayed with whatever the Contact record currently says, and this is acceptable for v1.
assumptions.rationale: Tracking historical roles needs a new multi-table model and manual upkeep; showing current data with the engagement date keeps the schema untouched.

success_criteria: The Country history panel loads the first page (50 rows) in under 2 seconds at p95 for the largest country in the CRM
100% of the ~100 countries render a history panel without errors, including countries with zero engagements (explicit empty state)
Zero new database tables and zero new required fields for Regional Coordinators in the release
In UAT, at least 5 project managers can find the most recent engagement and any active missions for a given country in under 30 seconds without help
The timeline never displays a row the viewing user cannot open on the underlying record (verified by permission test suite covering Country/Mission/Contact access cases, 0 leaks)
Within 60 days of release, at least 60% of new missions are created by a PM who opened the history panel in the same session (measured from existing usage logs)

challenges.challenge_text: The timeline joins Engagement, Mission, Project and Contact rows, but a PM sees a row only if they can open the underlying record. Row-level checks are ambiguous when the records have different permissions. Example: a PM on Mission X for Country Y can open the Mission, but the linked Engagement is a confidential ministerial meeting held under another team's access. Rows could be shown with partial data, or a contact name could be shown while the engagement is hidden. Counts, the 'N engagements' summary in the New Mission flow, the 'Active missions' banner and pagination totals would also leak the existence of restricted records. The criterion 'never displays a row the user cannot open' does not cover aggregates, hidden-row gaps, or the case where the Mission is visible but the linked Contact is not. Also, 'some access to Country records' means a PM with access to one mission in a country could see the full history of every other team's engagements there. That breaks least-privilege and lets a PM see another country team's notes.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: Round 1: the Proposer defers to the existing access model, which assumes it already enforces least-privilege at record level and works when composed across entities. That is unverified.

challenges.challenge_text: Contacts are shown with their current record data next to historical engagement dates. If a minister or ministry official has been replaced, a 2022 engagement row will show the new person's name and title against a meeting they never attended. This misleads the PM about who the counterpart was. PMs may then reach out to the wrong ministry contact or assume the wrong relationship exists. A deactivated or departed contact may also be displayed with no stale marker. Across ~100 countries with frequent turnover, this is the main failure mode of the feature, not an edge case. A cheap mitigation exists without a new schema: store or show the contact name as recorded on the engagement, or flag rows where the contact record was modified or deactivated after the engagement date.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: Round 1: the Proposer accepts that history shows current contact data and calls this acceptable for v1, but gives no mitigation for misattribution.

challenges.challenge_text: The proposal says rows with missing country links are shown as gaps, but a record can only be shown on a country timeline if the query can reach it. An Engagement that lacks a direct country_id and has no Contact, Mission or Project link will be silently excluded. An Engagement linked via a Contact is attributed to the Contact's current country, not the country where the engagement took place. After a contact moves ministries or countries, past engagements may move to the wrong timeline or vanish from the right one. A PM who sees a clean 'no prior engagement' state for a country may start a mission that duplicates or conflicts with earlier outreach. The 'single query' claim also hides multi-path attribution, which can cause double-counted or missing rows. The panel is labelled 'full history' but has no completeness indicator, such as a count of unlinked records or a data-quality caveat. This makes false reassurance the likely outcome.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: Round 1: the Proposer treats gaps as 'visible', but records that fail the join are invisible by construction. The claim does not hold.

challenges.challenge_text: The panel is described as advisory and non-blocking, but the 'Active missions in this country' banner is the only signal of an existing mission in the same country. Where the PM lacks access to another team's mission, that mission is filtered out under the permission-inheritance rule. The banner will then show nothing, which tells the PM that no one else is working there. Two teams can then approach the same ministry in parallel with conflicting asks, a diplomatic risk. The empty state and the banner need to distinguish 'none exist' from 'none visible to you', for example a count-only or 'restricted mission exists' indicator. That indicator in turn has to be reconciled with the confidentiality concern in C1. The design must choose one behaviour deliberately rather than by accident.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: Round 1: the Proposer frames the feature as orientation, not a control, but the banner is used as a safety signal and fails silently under least-privilege filtering.

challenges.challenge_text: The proposal assumes each country has hundreds to low thousands of rows, with a 2-second p95 target for the largest country. Permission filtering is applied per row across the Engagement, Mission and Contact joins, so the query cannot rely on the country_id and date indexes alone. If access checks run in application code after the fetch, pagination breaks: a page of 50 can return 12 visible rows, or total counts are computed before filtering and leak or mislead. Large countries with long histories and heavy restricted content will be the slowest and most inconsistent. No data volume has actually been measured, and the free-text 'summary' field is rendered with no check for sensitive notes appearing in the timeline view.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: Round 1: the Proposer's performance assumption ignores the cost and pagination effects of per-row permission enforcement.

Deterministic country attribution with fixed precedence: Engagement.country_id, then linked Mission's country, then linked Project's country, then linked Contact's country. Rows are deduplicated by record ID so multi-path links never double-count

'Active missions' banner shows visible active missions in full, plus a count-only line 'N more active missions exist that you cannot view — contact Country Operations'. It shows no names, teams or details. The restricted count is a PM-facing default that needs human sign-off (see C4 response)

Pagination (default 50 rows) with keyset pagination on (date, id) over the permission-filtered set
Non-blocking: the New Mission flow shows the history link and visible-row summary but requires no acknowledgement

New data-entry fields or required manual steps for Regional Coordinators

AI/ML summarization, sentiment or 'relationship health' scores, recommendations

Cross-country or regional rollups

assumptions.statement: 'Full history' means all Engagement, Mission and Project-affiliation records already in the CRM that can be linked to the country, not external systems or undocumented interactions.
assumptions.rationale: Limiting to stored records means no ingestion or data entry, so the team can ship in one cycle.

assumptions.statement: Row visibility follows the existing record-level access model, applied as a query predicate, and a row is visible only if its primary record is openable. Whether a PM with access to one mission in a country should see other teams' country history at all is an institutional access-policy decision that needs human confirmation. v1 ships with whatever the existing Country/Mission model already grants.
assumptions.rationale: Query-level enforcement gives consistent rows, counts and pagination without new RBAC. Policy on cross-team visibility is not a product decision and is flagged for a human owner.

assumptions.statement: The panel is an advisory orientation aid, not a compliance control. The banner is a best-effort signal and says explicitly when restricted active missions exist.
assumptions.rationale: Advisory behavior avoids approval workflows. A count-only restricted indicator stops the banner from implying 'nobody else is working here'.

assumptions.statement: Engagements can be attributed to a country through a fixed precedence of existing links (direct country, Mission, Project, Contact), deduplicated by record ID. Records with no reachable link are excluded and the UI says so in a static caveat.
assumptions.rationale: A deterministic rule avoids double counting and needs no schema change or cleanup. Honest caveat copy prevents false reassurance at zero cost.

assumptions.statement: Per-country volume is hundreds to low thousands of rows and permission predicates can be pushed into the indexed query. This is verified on a production-sized copy before release rather than assumed.
assumptions.rationale: Avoids caching or materialized views in v1. A measurement gate catches the risk cheaply.

assumptions.statement: Contacts show their current record data, with a deterministic stale marker when the Contact was modified or deactivated after the engagement date. Point-in-time role history is not tracked.
assumptions.rationale: Uses existing updated_at and status fields only. It warns PMs about possible misattribution without a role-history model or coordinator upkeep.

success_criteria: The first page (50 rows) loads in under 2 seconds at p95 for the largest country, measured on a production-sized copy with realistic restricted-row mix, before release
100% of ~100 countries render without errors, including an explicit empty state that carries the 'unlinked/restricted records not included' caveat
Zero new database tables and zero new required fields for Regional Coordinators
In UAT, at least 5 PMs find the most recent engagement and any active missions for a country in under 30 seconds unaided

Permission test suite with 0 leaks across rows, linked Contact/Project names, summary text, row totals, page counts and the 'N engagements' summary, covering: Mission visible/Engagement hidden, Mission visible/Contact hidden, and PM with access to a single mission in the country
Every page returns exactly 50 rows unless it is the last page, and the displayed total equals the count of rows the user can open (0 discrepancies in test data with 30%+ restricted rows)
Test: a Contact modified or deactivated after an engagement date always shows the stale marker on that row, and a Contact unchanged since then never shows it (100% on fixture data)
Test: an Engagement reachable by multiple link paths appears exactly once and under the precedence-determined country
Test: the active-missions banner shows the restricted count line whenever a restricted active mission exists in the country, and never exposes its name, team or details
Within 60 days of release, at least 60% of new missions are created by a PM who opened the history panel in the same session (from existing usage logs)

challenge_responses.response: Accepted as a defect in the spec, with a fix that adds no tables, screens or coordinator steps. (1) Permission predicate runs inside the single SQL query, so rows, totals, page counts and the 'N engagements' summary all come from the same filtered set and none can leak hidden-record existence. (2) A row appears only if the primary record (Engagement or Mission) is openable. A linked Contact or Project the user cannot open is replaced by a 'Restricted' placeholder rather than showing a name next to a hidden record. (3) Success criteria now cover aggregates, hidden-contact and hidden-engagement cases. Not resolved by me: whether a PM with one mission in a country should see other teams' engagements in that country is an access-policy and data-classification decision. v1 inherits the existing Country/Mission access model unchanged, and I am routing that question to a human policy owner. I will not invent a new rule or build custom RBAC.

Agreed this is the main failure mode, and the cheap fix needs no schema change. Each row compares the engagement date to the existing Contact modified-at and status fields. If the Contact was modified or deactivated after the engagement, the row shows a 'Contact record changed since this engagement' marker, plus a 'Deactivated' tag where relevant. This is a pure display computation with no new fields, tables, or coordinator input. I am not adding point-in-time role history or snapshotting names onto engagements, since that is a new multi-table model or manual upkeep. The marker is conservative: it over-flags harmless edits such as a phone number change, so the wording says 'may differ' and not 'was replaced'.

Partially defended. Records with no link to any Country, Mission, Project or Contact cannot be attributed to any country, so there is nothing to count per country. A computed 'unlinked records' indicator is impossible at country level, and a global one would need data-quality tooling or backfill, which is out of scope. What I do change, at zero schema cost, is: a fixed attribution precedence (direct country, then Mission, then Project, then Contact) with dedupe by record ID, which removes double-counting. A mandatory footer and empty-state caveat says the view shows linked records only and is not proof of no prior contact. Contact-derived attribution is kept as the last fallback because dropping it would hide more history, not less. The remaining risk is a data-quality issue that needs owners to clean the data. I am not putting that on Regional Coordinators in this release.

Accepted: the banner must not fail silently. The design choice is deliberate. The active-missions banner shows visible missions in full and adds a count-only line, 'N more active missions exist that you cannot view — contact Country Operations', with no name, team or details. This leaks only that a restricted active mission exists, which is the minimum needed to prevent parallel approaches to the same ministry. Engagement and contact rows get no such hidden-count indicator, so C1's leakage concern holds for them. It is a template change on an existing query, with no new screen, table or configuration. Whether disclosing the existence of a restricted mission is acceptable is a diplomatic and security-classification decision, not mine. I am flagging it for a human owner, and if they say no, the line is removed and the footer caveat remains.

The failure the Critic describes (post-fetch filtering breaking pagination and totals) only happens if checks run in application code, and v1 does not do that. The access scope is applied as a predicate in the same query that paginates and counts, using keyset pagination on (date, id) over the filtered set. A page is always full unless it is the last page, and totals come from the filtered set only, so nothing leaks. Indexes on country_id and date still drive the scan, with the permission predicate as an additional filter, at hundreds to low thousands of rows per country. The assumption is turned into a pre-release measurement gate on a production-sized copy with a realistic restricted-row mix, so unmeasured volume is checked before release. No caching, materialized views or new infrastructure are needed. The summary field is shown only when the Engagement is openable, so it has the same access as the record itself. Whether summary text needs sensitivity redaction is a data-classification question for a human owner, not a product feature I will build in v1.

challenges.challenge_text: Engineering gaps are closed: the permission predicate runs in the same query as rows, totals and pagination, rows appear only if the primary record is openable, and linked Contact/Project names are replaced by 'Restricted' placeholders. What remains is whether a PM with access to one mission in a country should see other teams' engagements in that country. That is an institutional access and classification decision that engineering cannot settle.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: The Proposer fixed the aggregate-leak, partial-row and hidden-contact cases and correctly declined to invent new RBAC. It routed the cross-team visibility question to a human policy owner. Further argument here would not help.

challenges.challenge_text: The risk was a 2022 engagement row showing a replaced minister's successor as the counterpart. The Proposer now flags any row whose Contact was modified or deactivated after the engagement date, with 'may differ' wording and a 'Deactivated' tag, and covers it with a fixture test.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: The revision uses existing updated_at and status fields and adds no schema or coordinator upkeep. It over-flags harmless edits, which could cause some alert fatigue, but the wording is non-alarming and over-flagging is the safe direction for an MVP. The risk is adequately bounded.

challenges.challenge_text: The static caveat, empty-state wording and deterministic precedence with dedupe resolve the false-reassurance and double-count concerns. One solvable gap remains. An Engagement attributed only via the Contact fallback lands on the Contact's current country. If a ministry official moved countries or posts, a past engagement from Country A appears in Country B's timeline as if it happened there, and may drop out of Country A's. A PM preparing a mission to B may misread that history. The row looks identical to directly attributed rows.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: The defense is sound on unreachable records, which cannot be counted by definition, and on the caveat. It does not address how contact-derived rows are shown. The fix is a display-only label on rows attributed via the fallback, such as 'Linked via contact's current country — may not reflect where this took place'. That needs no schema change, backfill or coordinator work.

challenges.challenge_text: The banner no longer implies that nobody else is working in the country. It adds a count-only line that reveals no name, team or details. Whether disclosing that a restricted active mission exists is acceptable is a diplomatic and security-classification decision.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: The Proposer made a deliberate design choice, kept it to the minimum disclosure, and explicitly flagged it for a human owner with a fallback to remove the line. Engineering cannot settle the remaining question.

challenges.challenge_text: The risks were post-fetch filtering breaking pagination and totals, unmeasured volume, and summary text exposure. The permission predicate now runs in the same query with keyset pagination on (date, id), and a production-sized measurement gate with a realistic restricted-row mix is a release criterion. Summary visibility is tied to the openable Engagement.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: The defense removes the pagination and count inconsistency, and the measurement gate bounds the performance risk cheaply. Summary text carries the same access as the record the user can already open, so it adds no new exposure. Redaction policy is a classification matter outside this MVP.

assumptions.statement: 'Full history' means all Engagement, Mission and Project-affiliation records already in the CRM that can be linked to the country, not external systems or undocumented interactions.
assumptions.rationale: Limiting to stored records means no ingestion or data entry, so the team can ship in one cycle.

assumptions.statement: Row visibility follows the existing record-level access model, applied as a query predicate, and a row is visible only if its primary record is openable. Whether a PM with access to one mission in a country should see other teams' country history at all is an institutional access-policy decision that needs human confirmation. v1 ships with whatever the existing Country/Mission model already grants.
assumptions.rationale: Query-level enforcement gives consistent rows, counts and pagination without new RBAC. Policy on cross-team visibility is not a product decision and is flagged for a human owner.

assumptions.statement: The panel is an advisory orientation aid, not a compliance control. The banner is a best-effort signal and says explicitly when restricted active missions exist, subject to human sign-off on disclosing that count.
assumptions.rationale: Advisory behavior avoids approval workflows. A count-only restricted indicator stops the banner from implying 'nobody else is working here'.

assumptions.statement: Engagements can be attributed to a country through a fixed precedence of existing links (direct country, Mission, Project, Contact), deduplicated by record ID. Rows attributed only via the Contact fallback carry a visible display-only label. Records with no reachable link are excluded and the UI says so in a static caveat.
assumptions.rationale: A deterministic rule avoids double counting and needs no schema change or cleanup. The label and caveat copy prevent misreading and false reassurance at zero data-entry cost.

assumptions.statement: Per-country volume is hundreds to low thousands of rows and permission predicates can be pushed into the indexed query. This is verified on a production-sized copy before release rather than assumed.
assumptions.rationale: Avoids caching or materialized views in v1. A measurement gate catches the risk cheaply.

assumptions.statement: Contacts show their current record data, with a deterministic stale marker when the Contact was modified or deactivated after the engagement date. Point-in-time role history is not tracked.
assumptions.rationale: Uses existing updated_at and status fields only. It warns PMs about possible misattribution without a role-history model or coordinator upkeep.

challenge_responses.response: The Critic is right about the remaining gap: a contact-derived row looks identical to directly attributed rows, so a PM preparing a mission to Country B could read a Country A engagement as having happened in B. The fix adds no screens, tables or coordinator steps. The attribution query already resolves which precedence branch matched, so rows that matched only via the Contact fallback get a label: "Linked via contact's current country — may not reflect where this took place". The footer and empty-state caveat now also say that contact-linked records appear under the contact's current country. I am keeping the defense on the rest. Records with no reachable link cannot be counted per country, so no 'unlinked records' indicator is possible. Re-attributing engagements to where they actually took place would need stored location data or manual correction, so it stays out of v1. The residual risk is that a contact-derived engagement may be missing from the original country's timeline. That is a data-quality limitation covered by the caveat, and fixing it needs data owners rather than a v1 feature.

challenges.challenge_text: Whether a PM with access to one mission in a country may see other teams' engagement history depends on institutional access policy. The row-level, aggregate and Contact/Project masking mechanics are now covered by in-query predicates and 'Restricted' rendering.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: The Proposer put the policy question in front of a human owner and ships with the existing access model. Engineering cannot settle the remaining question. Status stays escalated.

challenges.challenge_text: Current contact data was shown next to historical engagement dates, so a replaced minister could appear against a meeting they never attended.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: The deterministic stale marker and 'Deactivated' tag, built from existing updated_at and status fields, adequately bound the risk for an MVP. It stays accepted.

challenges.challenge_text: Original risk: contact-derived engagements sit under the contact's current country, and a clean empty state falsely reassures a PM that no prior outreach exists.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: The Proposer closed the remaining engineering gap with a per-row 'Linked via contact's current country' label and a footer and empty-state caveat. A fixture test also covers a contact who moved from Country A to Country B. A contact-derived engagement can still be missing from its original country's timeline, and unlinked records can't be counted. Fixing that needs stored location data or data-owner cleanup, which is correctly out of v1 scope. The caveat bounds the residual risk adequately for an MVP.

challenges.challenge_text: Disclosing the count of restricted active missions has to be weighed against the confidentiality concern in C1. Whether to show that count is a diplomatic disclosure policy decision.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: The design makes a deliberate choice, a count-only line with no names or details. It also has a fallback of removing the line if the policy owner says no. The decision belongs to a human policy owner, so it stays escalated.

challenges.challenge_text: Post-fetch permission filtering could break pagination and totals, and volume had not been measured.
challenges.evaluation_of_proposer: Permission predicates now run in the same query as selection, pagination and counting. Keyset pagination is in place, and a release-gate measurement on a production-sized copy is required. The risk is adequately bounded, so it stays accepted.

C1.challenge_text: The timeline joins Engagement, Mission, Project and Contact rows, but a PM sees a row only if they can open the underlying record. Row-level checks are ambiguous when the records have different permissions. Example: a PM on Mission X for Country Y can open the Mission, but the linked Engagement is a confidential ministerial meeting held under another team's access. Rows could be shown with partial data, or a contact name could be shown while the engagement is hidden. Counts, the 'N engagements' summary in the New Mission flow, the 'Active missions' banner and pagination totals would also leak the existence of restricted records. The criterion 'never displays a row the user cannot open' does not cover aggregates, hidden-row gaps, or the case where the Mission is visible but the linked Contact is not. Also, 'some access to Country records' means a PM with access to one mission in a country could see the full history of every other team's engagements there. That breaks least-privilege and lets a PM see another country team's notes.

C2.challenge_text: Contacts are shown with their current record data next to historical engagement dates. If a minister or ministry official has been replaced, a 2022 engagement row will show the new person's name and title against a meeting they never attended. This misleads the PM about who the counterpart was. PMs may then reach out to the wrong ministry contact or assume the wrong relationship exists. A deactivated or departed contact may also be displayed with no stale marker. Across ~100 countries with frequent turnover, this is the main failure mode of the feature, not an edge case. A cheap mitigation exists without a new schema: store or show the contact name as recorded on the engagement, or flag rows where the contact record was modified or deactivated after the engagement date.

C3.challenge_text: The proposal says rows with missing country links are shown as gaps, but a record can only be shown on a country timeline if the query can reach it. An Engagement that lacks a direct country_id and has no Contact, Mission or Project link will be silently excluded. An Engagement linked via a Contact is attributed to the Contact's current country, not the country where the engagement took place. After a contact moves ministries or countries, past engagements may move to the wrong timeline or vanish from the right one. A PM who sees a clean 'no prior engagement' state for a country may start a mission that duplicates or conflicts with earlier outreach. The 'single query' claim also hides multi-path attribution, which can cause double-counted or missing rows. The panel is labelled 'full history' but has no completeness indicator, such as a count of unlinked records or a data-quality caveat. This makes false reassurance the likely outcome.

C4.challenge_text: The panel is described as advisory and non-blocking, but the 'Active missions in this country' banner is the only signal of an existing mission in the same country. Where the PM lacks access to another team's mission, that mission is filtered out under the permission-inheritance rule. The banner will then show nothing, which tells the PM that no one else is working there. Two teams can then approach the same ministry in parallel with conflicting asks, a diplomatic risk. The empty state and the banner need to distinguish 'none exist' from 'none visible to you', for example a count-only or 'restricted mission exists' indicator. That indicator in turn has to be reconciled with the confidentiality concern in C1. The design must choose one behaviour deliberately rather than by accident.

C5.challenge_text: The proposal assumes each country has hundreds to low thousands of rows, with a 2-second p95 target for the largest country. Permission filtering is applied per row across the Engagement, Mission and Contact joins, so the query cannot rely on the country_id and date indexes alone. If access checks run in application code after the fetch, pagination breaks: a page of 50 can return 12 visible rows, or total counts are computed before filtering and leak or mislead. Large countries with long histories and heavy restricted content will be the slowest and most inconsistent. No data volume has actually been measured, and the free-text 'summary' field is rendered with no check for sensitive notes appearing in the timeline view.

final_decision.feature_request: Project managers should be able to see the full history of engagement with a country before starting a new mission.
final_decision.executive_summary: v1 is a read-only Country Engagement History panel on the Country record and as a pre-flight step in the New Mission flow. It shows a reverse-chronological timeline built only from existing Engagement, Mission, Project and Contact records, with no new tables, no new fields and no coordinator work. The main trade-off argued was completeness and safety against a no-schema, no-RBAC MVP. Permission checks run inside the query, contact rows carry staleness and attribution labels, and a caveat says the view is not proof of no prior contact. Two questions need a human decision: whether PMs may see other teams' engagement history in a country (C1), and whether the banner may disclose that restricted active missions exist (C4).

open_questions_for_humans: [C1] Access-policy owner (e.g., Head of Diplomatic Security or Legal): Should a PM who has access to one mission in a country be able to see other teams' engagement history in that country under the existing Country/Mission access model, or must v1 restrict this further? The panel's row visibility depends on this answer; v1 currently ships with the existing model unchanged.

[C4] Head of Diplomatic Security (diplomatic/security classification owner): May the 'Active missions' banner show a count-only line ('N more active missions exist that you cannot view — contact Country Operations') revealing that restricted active missions exist, with no names, teams or details? If yes, the line is added to scope; if no, the line is removed and only the footer caveat remains.
